name: Madelung deformity
aliases: radial physeal dysplasia of the wrist

reference.source: Green's Operative Hand Surgery / Tachdjian's Pediatric Orthopaedics
clinicalPearls: A growth disturbance of the volar-ulnar part of the distal radial physis produces progressive volar and ulnar tilt of the distal radial articular surface
The distal ulna becomes dorsally prominent and subluxed, the radius bows, and the carpus (with the lunate at its apex) sinks into a V-shaped notch between radius and ulna
It is typically bilateral, more common in adolescent girls, and usually presents in the second decade with wrist pain, deformity, and reduced extension and rotation
A tethering anomalous volar radiolunate ligament (Vickers ligament) crosses the deficient physis and contributes to the progressive deformity
There is a strong association with Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis and with mutations or deletions of the SHOX gene, which also cause mesomelic short stature
Radiographs show the characteristic volar and ulnar tilt of the distal radius, triangulation of the carpus, and dorsal ulnar prominence

Management ranges from observation and activity modification to surgery: release of the Vickers ligament with physiolysis in the growing child, or corrective radial osteotomy (often with ulnar shortening) once skeletally mature
reference.pathophysiology: Madelung deformity results from a localised dysplasia and premature growth arrest of the volar-ulnar quadrant of the distal radial physis. Continued growth of the dorsal-radial portion of the physis, combined with tethering by a thick anomalous volar ligament (Vickers ligament) running from the radius to the lunate, produces progressive volar and ulnar angulation of the distal radial joint surface. Relative overgrowth of the ulna leads to dorsal ulnar prominence and carpal triangulation. Many cases are genetically determined through SHOX haploinsufficiency, as seen in Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, which links the wrist deformity to a wider skeletal dysplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple hereditary exostoses affecting the distal forearm
Rickets or other metabolic bone disease with wrist deformity
additionalInvestigations: Posteroanterior and lateral wrist radiographs to assess radial tilt, ulnar variance, and carpal triangulation
MRI to demonstrate the anomalous Vickers ligament and any physeal bar
CT for detailed bony assessment when planning an osteotomy
Assessment of stature and limb proportions with SHOX gene testing where dyschondrosteosis is suspected
Bilateral wrist imaging given the frequent bilateral involvement
redFlags: Rapidly progressive deformity or pain during the adolescent growth spurt
Signs of ulnar impaction or distal radioulnar joint instability
Features suggesting an underlying skeletal dysplasia that warrants genetic evaluation
reference.prognosis: Progression tends to occur during skeletal growth and then stabilises at maturity; early ligament release with physiolysis can halt progression in the growing child, while corrective osteotomy in the mature wrist reliably improves pain and appearance, although some loss of rotation may persist.
pitfalls: Mistaking early Madelung deformity for a simple wrist sprain and missing its progression
Failing to release the Vickers ligament, allowing continued tethering after bony surgery
Not recognising the association with SHOX-related short stature (dyschondrosteosis)
Operating on skeletally immature bone without addressing the physeal tether
